opus-5.5.text:
I feel quite good about it, honestly. When we first decided to go with MTP, multi-token prediction, there was real debate inside the team. It adds complexity to training, and at the time it wasn't obvious that the gains would justify the extra engineering cost. Some people worried it might hurt the main next-token objective, or that the benefits would only show up at small scale and disappear as the model got bigger.

What convinced us was thinking about it from two angles. The first is training signal. If you ask the model to predict not just the next token but a few tokens further ahead, you force it to plan a little, to form representations that carry more information about where the sequence is going. In our experiments, that seemed to give a denser, richer learning signal, especially for things like code and math where structure matters.

The second angle is inference. Those extra prediction heads can be reused for speculative decoding. The model drafts several tokens at once and then verifies them, so you get a real speedup in generation without changing output quality. For us, efficiency has always been a core value. We don't have unlimited compute, so anything that gives you both better training and cheaper serving is very attractive.

Looking back, I think it was the right call. It's not a magic trick. It's one of many small design choices that add up. But it reflects the way we like to work: question the default recipe everyone uses, run careful experiments, and if something holds up, commit to it even if it's not the mainstream choice yet. If I'm being honest, I'm a bit proud that the team was willing to take that risk.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I feel good about it, but I want to be careful about how I say that, because it wasn't an obvious call at the time.

Multi-token prediction was something we'd looked at for a while. The idea is simple: instead of only asking the model to predict the very next token, you also ask it to predict a couple of tokens further ahead during training. On paper that gives you a denser training signal and pushes the model to plan a little more, rather than just greedily choosing what comes next. In practice, a lot of people tried versions of it and got mixed results. So when we were deciding, there was real risk. If it didn't help, we'd have spent compute and engineering time on an extra head that just sits there.

What tipped it for us was two things. First, our small-scale ablations were consistent. It wasn't a huge jump, but it moved in the same direction every time, on reasoning-heavy benchmarks especially, and I trust a small, stable signal more than a big noisy one. Second, the inference story. Once you have those extra prediction heads, you can use them for speculative decoding essentially for free. So even in the worst case where the training benefit was marginal, we'd still get faster generation. That asymmetry made the decision much easier for me.

The part I underestimated was the engineering. Keeping the MTP module stable at scale, making sure it didn't interfere with the main objective, getting the loss weighting right so it helped rather than distracted. Those details took longer than we expected. If you asked me what I'd do differently, I would have invested earlier in the infrastructure for it, instead of treating it as a late add-on.

But the result? The model came out stronger on the things we care about, and decoding got faster. So yes, I'm glad we did it. I'd just say to anyone considering it: don't do it because it's fashionable. Run the ablations, make sure you're seeing the signal yourself, and plan for the fact that it's more work than the paper makes it look.

Looking back, I think it was a good decision. With multi-token prediction, the intuition is that we want the model to learn more than just the next immediate step—we want it to anticipate what comes after that, too. That gives it a richer learning signal.

Of course, that benefit has to justify the added training complexity. So I’d judge the choice by whether it improves the final model in practice, rather than by how elegant the idea sounds.
